guide.summary: Synthesize Ideas in AP Research means designing and justifying a method, collecting and analyzing data, and drawing conclusions that add new understanding while honestly acknowledging limitations.

sections.heading: Choosing and justifying a method
sections.body: Common methods: experiments (manipulate a variable and compare randomly assigned groups; strongest for causation), quasi-experiments (compare existing groups), surveys (measure attitudes or behaviors in larger samples; good for describing and correlating), interviews and focus groups (in-depth perspectives), content or discourse analysis (systematic study of texts, media, or documents), case studies (an in-depth look at one case), and mixed methods. The method section explains what you did in enough detail that someone could replicate it and why this method fits your question better than alternatives, often citing studies that used similar methods. Sampling matters: random samples support generalization; convenience samples (like social media recruitment) are easier but may be biased; purposive samples select people with specific characteristics for qualitative depth.

sections.heading: Analyzing data and drawing conclusions
sections.body: Plan analysis in advance. Quantitative analysis might compare means, compute correlations, or run significance tests; present results in clear tables or graphs. Qualitative analysis codes data into themes, supported by representative quotations. Report results before interpreting them. Conclusions must match the design: the screen-time survey shows an association, and open-ended responses suggest mechanisms (notifications, losing track of time), but self-reported data from a convenience sample can't establish causation or represent all students. Mixed data can be powerful: the numbers show a pattern, and the qualitative responses help explain it.

sections.heading: Limitations and new understanding
sections.body: Every study has limitations: sample size and type, self-report bias, measurement validity, confounding variables, a short time frame, or a single setting. Stating limitations clearly, along with how they affect interpretation, increases credibility. The discussion should explain how your findings relate to prior research (confirming, extending, or contradicting it), what new understanding your study contributes (even a small, local contribution counts), implications for practice or policy, and directions for future research that address your limitations.

keyTakeaways: Match the method to the question; justify it.
Limitations and future research are required.
examTips: Cite prior studies that used your method to justify it.
Use tables and figures with clear labels.
Explicitly state the new understanding in your conclusion.
guide.cramSheet:
**Methods:** experiment · quasi-experiment · survey · interview/focus group · content analysis · case study · mixed

**Sampling:** random · convenience · purposive · size

**Analysis:** means · correlation · significance · coding/themes · tables/graphs

**Discussion:** relate to prior research · new understanding · implications · limitations · future research

practice.prompt: Write a method justification for a study answering: 'How do first-year teachers at three local high schools describe the support they receive in their first semester?'

rubric.description: Chooses a fitting method (semi-structured interviews or focus groups).
Explains why it fits better than alternatives, ideally citing similar prior use.
Describes purposive sampling and replicable procedures.

practice.sampleResponse:
A. Semi-structured interviews.

B. Because the question asks how teachers describe their experiences, interviews capture detailed perspectives a survey would miss, while a semi-structured format keeps questions consistent across participants. Previous studies of new-teacher induction have used interviews for the same reason.

C. I will purposively sample all first-year teachers at three high schools (about 9–12 people), conduct 30-minute recorded interviews with the same core questions and follow-ups, transcribe them, and code them for themes.

practice.prompt: Write part of the discussion section for the screen-time study.

parts.label: C
parts.prompt: State the new understanding and a future study.

rubric.description: Relates findings to prior research (confirming or extending), stated generally if no sources given.
States the contribution and a specific future study addressing a limitation.

practice.sampleResponse:
A. Students who reported more than four hours of recreational screen time reported almost an hour less sleep than those with under two hours, and their own explanations point to notifications and losing track of time.

B. This pattern is consistent with prior research linking evening device use to shorter sleep, and it extends that work by documenting the pattern and students' own explanations at our school.

C. The study contributes local evidence that school leaders could use for sleep education. Future research should use sleep trackers and randomly assign students to a nighttime phone limit to test whether reducing screen time causes more sleep.

practice.prompt: Describe how to present the screen-time results in the paper.

parts.label: C
parts.prompt: Describe how to present qualitative responses.

rubric.description: Proposes an appropriate graph or table with labeled axes and units.
Writes results that report without interpreting.
Presents qualitative data with themes and representative quotes, protecting identity.

practice.sampleResponse:
A. A bar graph with screen-time categories (under 2, 2–4, over 4 hours) on the x-axis and mean school-night sleep hours on the y-axis, with the number of respondents in each group labeled.

B. 'Respondents reporting more than 4 hours of daily recreational screen time reported a mean of 6.4 hours of sleep on school nights, compared with 7.3 hours among those reporting under 2 hours.'

C. Group open-ended responses into themes, such as 'losing track of time' and 'nighttime notifications,' report how many respondents mentioned each, and include short anonymous quotations identified by participant number.

practice.prompt: Write the limitations paragraph for the screen-time study.

rubric.description: Names at least two specific limitations.
Notes how future studies could address them.

practice.sampleResponse: This study has several limitations. First, respondents were recruited through social media, so students who use social media more may be overrepresented, and the results may not represent all students at the school. Second, screen time and sleep were self-reported, and students often misestimate both, which could exaggerate or hide the true relationship. Third, the survey design cannot establish causation; other factors, such as homework load or anxiety, might lead to both more screen time and less sleep. Future studies could use random sampling, phone screen-time reports and sleep trackers, and an experimental design to address these issues.
